questions.stem: The central argument of the passage is that:
options: Routine, framework-preserving work is essential to progress, yet the very consensus that enables it can blind a science to contrary evidence until anomalies force a crisis.
Scientists are fundamentally dishonest about their data.
Scientific revolutions happen suddenly and without warning.
A mature science should abandon its framework whenever a single observation fails to fit.
questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.passage: For most of its working life, a mature science behaves less like a restless explorer than like a careful accountant. Its practitioners are not, on the whole, trying to overturn the framework they inherited; they are trying to extend it, to tidy its edges, to force reluctant observations into the boxes the theory has already prepared. This unglamorous labour is not a failing but the very condition of progress: only a community that agrees on what counts as a legitimate problem, and on what would count as a solution, can accumulate the fine-grained results on which any deeper understanding must rest. Yet the same agreement that makes such precision possible also breeds a peculiar blindness. Observations that refuse to fit are, for a long time, not so much rejected as unseen — set aside as errors of measurement, as noise, as problems for someone else on some later day. An anomaly becomes a crisis only when it can no longer be quarantined, when it multiplies and begins to touch the framework's load-bearing assumptions. It is at that point, and rarely before, that a discipline becomes willing to entertain the once-unthinkable thought that the trouble lies not in the stubborn facts but in the theory itself. The revolutions we later celebrate as sudden were, almost always, preceded by years in which the decisive evidence sat in plain view and was simply not counted.

questions.stem: The passage uses the pasture chiefly as:
options: An illustration of how individually rational choices can produce a collectively ruinous outcome when costs are shared but gains are private.
A nostalgic image of a vanished rural way of life.
A literal argument about the best way to raise cattle.
Evidence that herdsmen are unusually greedy people.
questions.subject: Reading Comprehension
questions.passage: Imagine a pasture open to all. Each herdsman, reasoning as any sensible person would, notices that adding one more animal to his own herd brings him the full value of that animal, while the cost of the extra grazing — the slow exhaustion of the common field — is shared among everyone. The private gain is concentrated and immediate; the public cost is diffuse and deferred. And so each herdsman, acting with impeccable individual rationality, adds another beast, and another, until the pasture that could have fed them all indefinitely is grazed to ruin. The tragedy, in the older and sterner sense of that word, is that it unfolds not through malice or stupidity but through the faithful pursuit of self-interest by people who can each see the ending and are each powerless, alone, to prevent it. What makes the problem so resistant to easy solution is that appeals to conscience are not merely ineffective but perverse: the herdsman who restrains himself for the common good simply cedes the grass to his less scrupulous neighbours, so that self-denial is punished and greed rewarded. This is why the more durable remedies have tended to involve not exhortation but structure — enforceable limits, assigned rights, mutual coercion mutually agreed upon — arrangements that change the arithmetic each individual faces rather than merely lecturing him about the sum.

questions.stem: The author calls the outcome a 'tragedy... in the older and sterner sense' to stress that the ruin results from:
options: The stupidity of herdsmen who cannot do arithmetic.
The inexorable working-out of rational self-interest, without malice or stupidity on anyone's part.
Random bad luck that no one could have foreseen.
A villain deliberately destroying the pasture.

questions.subject: Cloze Passage
questions.passage: The popular image of the inventor as a lone genius, struck by inspiration in a flash of solitary brilliance, is almost entirely a (63)________. Study the history of any major invention and you will find not a single moment of revelation but a long, (64)________ chain of small improvements, most of them made by people whose names have been forgotten. Each innovator (65)________ on the work of predecessors, often without fully realising how much he owed them. What we (66)________ to a single mind is usually the visible peak of an invisible mountain of collective effort. This is not to (67)________ the contribution of the exceptional individual, whose particular gift may be to see how scattered pieces fit together. But it is to insist that such a person works within, and depends (68)________, a community and a tradition. The myth of the solitary genius (69)________ because it flatters us with a simple story, and because a single hero is easier to celebrate than a diffuse network of contributors. Reality, as so often, is (70)________ tidy than the legend. Progress is less a series of thunderbolts than a slow (71)________ of countless hands, and the honest historian must resist the temptation to (72)________ that untidy truth into a more satisfying tale.
questions.direction: Select the most appropriate word for each blank in the passage.
